Rebuker
ree-BYOO-kur
n. (one who reproves sharply; a title God claims toward a nation that would not hear)
From Old North French rebuker, to beat back — re-, back, and buchier, to strike or fell timber. A rebuke is a blow that stops a man rather than one that destroys him. In Hosea it renders Hebrew musar, chastening instruction.

Biblical Definition

Hosea 5 is addressed to priests, to the house of Israel and to the house of the king, and the charge is that they have been a snare and a net to the people. In the middle of it God says something almost wistful: the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I have been a rebuker of them all. They were deep in their wickedness — profound, the word suggests going down into it — and the whole time God had been rebuking. The title is therefore an act of mercy that was refused. Rebuke in Scripture is never contempt; it is a blow struck to stop a man walking off a cliff. The risen Christ says it to a church he is about to spit out of his mouth: As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent. The rebuke is evidence of the love, not an interruption of it. Proverbs marks the dividing line between the two kinds of men: reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee; rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee. And Paul lays the duty on the ministry — reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all longsuffering and doctrine — joining the sharpness to patience and to teaching, so that it may never be mistaken for temper.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one that rebukes; a chider; one that reprehends or reproves with sharpness.

expand to see more

REBUKER, n. One that rebukes; a chider; one that reprehends.

REBUKE, v.t. To chide; to reprove; to reprehend for a fault; to check by reproof.

REPROVE, v.t. To blame; to censure; to charge with a fault to the face.

CHASTEN, v.t. To correct by punishment; to punish; to inflict pain for the purpose of reclaiming an offender.

LONGSUFFERING, n. Bearing injuries or provocation for a long time; patient; not easily provoked.

Key Scripture

Hosea 5:2 — "And the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I have been a rebuker of them all."

Revelation 3:19 — "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent."

Proverbs 9:8 — "Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee."

2 Timothy 4:2 — "Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine."

Modern Corruption

Rebuke is treated as incompatible with love, so it is either abolished as harmful or performed without the longsuffering and doctrine Paul binds to it; Christ says he rebukes the ones he loves.

expand to see more

The governing assumption of the age is that to correct someone is to harm them, and that acceptance is the only recognised form of love. Under that rule the pulpit goes quiet, church discipline lapses, and friends watch each other walk into ruin while congratulating themselves on being non-judgmental. Christ, writing to Laodicea, says the opposite in seven words: as many as I love, I rebuke and chasten. The letter is the sharpest in Revelation and it is addressed to people he calls beloved. A church that has abolished rebuke has not become more loving; it has quietly decided that nothing anyone does matters enough to mention.

The corrective has its own abuse. Paul does not say rebuke and stop; he says reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine — three verbs bound to two conditions. Longsuffering means the rebuker has borne with the man a long while and is not relieving his own irritation. Doctrine means the rebuke is from Scripture and not from taste. Where either is missing, what results is temper wearing the clothes of faithfulness, and Proverbs warns it will accomplish nothing anyway: the scorner will hate you, and only the wise man will love you for it. God himself was a rebuker of Israel for generations before the judgment fell.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew musar (H4148), chastening instruction; yakach (H3198), to reprove or argue a case; Greek elegcho (G1651), to convict or expose; epitimao (G2008), to rebuke sharply.

expand to see more

Hebrew musar (H4148) — discipline, chastening, instruction; behind a rebuker of them all.

Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to reprove, to argue, to decide a case; rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee.

Greek elegcho (G1651) — to convict, to expose to the light; rendered reprove, and used of the Spirit convicting the world.

Greek epitimao (G2008) — to censure sharply; used of Christ rebuking fevers, winds and devils.

Greek paideuo (G3811) — to train a child by discipline; the chasten paired with rebuke in Revelation 3.

Usage

"“I have been a rebuker of them all” — mercy offered and refused for generations."

"“As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten” — the rebuke as evidence of the love."

"“with all longsuffering and doctrine” — the two conditions on the duty."
